```text
domain:
    # Logical matrix dimensions
    i: dim in [0, NI)          # rows of A and C
    j: dim in [0, NJ)          # columns of B and C
    k: dim in [0, NK)          # shared inner dimension of A and B

data:
    # All matrices are dense, single-precision/ double-precision (DATA_TYPE = num_t).

    # A: NI x NK, accessed as A[i, k]
    # Layout chosen row-major in k for good spatial locality when k is innermost.
    A[i, k]: out/in num_t = (i, k) -> i * NK + k
        # "out/in" because A is written during initialization and read in GEMM.

    # B: NK x NJ, accessed as B[k, j]
    # Layout CHANGED vs original code: we store B column-major in (k, j),
    # i.e., contiguous in k for fixed j. This matches a k-innermost GEMM and
    # makes both A[i, k] and B[k, j] contiguous in the reduction dimension k.
    B[k, j]: out/in num_t = (k, j) -> j * NK + k

    # C: NI x NJ, accessed as C[i, j]
    # Layout: row-major in j for good spatial locality when j is innermost.
    C[i, j]: out/inout num_t = (i, j) -> i * NJ + j
        # "out/inout": written in initialization, then updated by GEMM.

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (from NI, NJ, NK macros)
    NI: size_t
    NJ: size_t
    NK: size_t

    # GEMM scalar parameters
    alpha: num_t
    beta:  num_t

    # Tunable blocking and vectorization parameters
    # TI, TJ: block (tile) sizes for i and j (outer loops)
    # TK:     block size for k (reduction dimension)
    # VJ:     SIMD width along j inside a tile (e.g., 4 or 8 for AVX)
    # UK:     unroll factor along k inside a tile
    TI: size_t
    TJ: size_t
    TK: size_t
    VJ: size_t
    UK: size_t

computation:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Initialization (matches init_array)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    # alpha = 1.5; beta = 1.2;
    set_scalars:
        alpha = (num_t)1.5
        beta  = (num_t)1.2

    # C[i][j] = ((i * j + 1) % NI) / NI
    init_C:
        for i in seq([0, NI)), j in seq([0, NJ)):
            C[i, j] = ((i * j + 1) mod NI) / (num_t)NI

    # A[i][k] = (i * (k + 1) % NK) / NK
    init_A:
        for i in seq([0, NI)), k in seq([0, NK)):
            A[i, k] = (i * (k + 1) mod NK) / (num_t)NK

    # B[k][j] = (k * (j + 2) % NJ) / NJ
    init_B:
        for k in seq([0, NK)), j in seq([0, NJ)):
            B[k, j] = (k * (j + 2) mod NJ) / (num_t)NJ

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. GEMM kernel
    #    Form C := alpha * A * B + beta * C
    #    A: NI x NK, B: NK x NJ, C: NI x NJ
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    gemm:
        # High-level mathematical specification matching kernel_gemm:
        # For each (i, j), scale C by beta and accumulate over k.
        for i, j:
            C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j] + alpha * sum(k in [0, NK), A[i, k] * B[k, j])

dependencies:
    # Initialization must complete before GEMM uses the matrices.
    for i in [0, NI), j in [0, NJ):
        init_C(i, j) -> gemm(i, j)
    for i in [0, NI), k in [0, NK):
        init_A(i, k) -> gemm(i, *)
    for k in [0, NK), j in [0, NJ):
        init_B(k, j) -> gemm(*, j)

optimization:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Loop blocking / tiling
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    # Block all three dimensions.  This creates tile indices I, J, K such that:
    #   i = I * TI + i_inner, j = J * TJ + j_inner, k = K * TK + k_inner
    # With partial tiles at the boundaries (handled by loop bounds).
    block(i, I, TI)
    block(j, J, TJ)
    block(k, K, TK)

    # Execute tiles in outer loops: I, then J, then K.
    # This produces a loop nest of the form:
    #   for I:
    #     for J:
    #       for K:
    #         for i in tile I:
    #           for j in tile J:
    #             acc = beta * C[i, j]
    #             for k in tile K:
    #               acc += alpha * A[i, k] * B[k, j]
    #             C[i, j] = acc       # after all K tiles
    #
    # This preserves the mathematical reduction over k, but improves cache
    # reuse of A-rows and B-columns within each (I, J, K) tile.
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)
    hoist(K)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Fusion of beta scaling and accumulation
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    # Instead of a separate pass:
    #   C[i,j] *= beta;
    #   C[i,j] += alpha * sum_k A[i,k] * B[k,j];
    # we implement:
    #   acc = beta * C[i,j];
    #   acc += alpha * sum_k A[i,k] * B[k,j];
    #   C[i,j] = acc;
    #
    # This:
    #  - eliminates a full extra traversal over C,
    #  - keeps C[i,j] in a register while accumulating over all K tiles,
    #  - reduces memory traffic on C.
    #
    # The fused form is already reflected in the high-level "computation"
    # equation for gemm.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Vectorization and unrolling
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    # Vectorize along the innermost j within each (i, K-tile) slice.
    # Because C is row-major (contiguous in j) and, for fixed (i, k),
    # B[k, j] is also contiguous in j *within a tile*, this enables
    # wide SIMD loads/stores on C and B and broadcast of A[i, k].
    vectorize(j, VJ)

    # Unroll the k-loop inside each tile to reduce loop overhead and
    # enable better instruction scheduling and FMA pairing.
    # UK should divide TK or be chosen so that the residual is handled
    # by a clean remainder loop.
    unroll(k, UK)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelization
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    # Parallelize across tiles in I and J.
    # Each (I, J) tile updates a disjoint submatrix C[i, j] with:
    #   i in [I * TI, min((I + 1) * TI, NI)),
    #   j in [J * TJ, min((J + 1) * TJ, NJ)).
    #
    # Since there are no cross-tile dependencies on C, it is safe to
    # execute these tiles in parallel.  K remains sequential inside each
    # tile to avoid race conditions on the reduction.
    parallelize(I)
    parallelize(J)
    # (An implementation may realize this as a 2D parallel-for over (I, J).)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Data-layout–aware choices
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    # - A is row-major in k; with k as the innermost reduction inside tiles,
    #   A[i, k] is streamed contiguously from memory for each fixed i.
    #
    # - B is explicitly chosen column-major (contiguous in k) so that
    #   B[k, j] is also streamed contiguously in k during the reduction.
    #   This matches a k-innermost design and gives both A and B good
    #   spatial locality in the reduction dimension.
    #
    # - C is row-major in j; with j innermost and vectorized, each SIMD
    #   operation works on a contiguous row segment of C.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Optional arithmetic micro-optimizations for initialization
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    # (Optional, if bitwise-identical results are not required.)
    #
    # Precompute reciprocals once and use multiplication instead of division
    # inside init loops:
    #   inv_NI = 1 / (num_t)NI
    #   inv_NJ = 1 / (num_t)NJ
    #   inv_NK = 1 / (num_t)NK
    #
    # then:
    #   C[i,j] = ((i * j + 1) mod NI) * inv_NI
    #   A[i,k] = (i * (k + 1) mod NK) * inv_NK
    #   B[k,j] = (k * (j + 2) mod NJ) * inv_NJ
    #
    # This hoists expensive divisions out of the inner loops at the cost
    # of one extra scalar division per dimension.  Small last-bit FP
    # differences are possible relative to using division directly.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Memory-usage constraints
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    # No additional full-size temporary matrices are introduced; all
    # optimizations operate in-place on A, B, and C using blocking and
    # register temporaries only.  Thus the memory footprint remains that
    # of the original program (3 * NI * NK/NJ elements) plus negligible
    # scalar or small-tile temporaries, well below the allowed +50%.
```

    # innermost reduction over k has unit-stride accesses in both A and B.

    # Row-major C: C[i, j] contiguous in j for fixed i
    C[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NJ + j

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE
    beta: DATA_TYPE

    TI: int  # tile size along i (e.g., 32–256 depending on L2/L3 size)
    TJ: int  # tile size along j
    TK: int  # tile size along k (panel width)

    # Tunable micro-kernel parameters
    VEC_K: int    # SIMD vector width in k (e.g., 8 for AVX2 float, 16 for AVX-512 float)
    UNROLL_J: int # unroll factor along j inside a tile (small, e.g., 2–8)

computation:
    # ---------------- Initialization (matches init_array) -------------------
    init_C:
        for i in [0, NI), j in [0, NJ):
            # C[i][j] = (i*j+1) % NI / NI

        for i in [0, NI), k in [0, NK):
            # A[i][k] = i*(k+1) % NK / NK
            A[i, k] = (i * (k + 1) mod NK) / NK

    init_B:
        for k in [0, NK), j in [0, NJ):
            # B[k][j] = k*(j+2) % NJ / NJ
            B[k, j] = (k * (j + 2) mod NJ) / NJ

    # ---------------- Main GEMM kernel (matches kernel_gemm) ---------------
    # Original kernel does, for each (i,j):
    #   1) C[i,j] *= beta
    #   2) C[i,j] += alpha * sum_k A[i,k] * B[k,j]
    #
    # The following single assignment is algebraically equivalent:
    #   C[i,j] = beta * C[i,j] + alpha * sum_k A[i,k] * B[k,j]
    # and corresponds to using a scalar accumulator in registers.
    gemm:
        for i in [0, NI), j in [0, NJ):
            C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j] +

optimization:
    # All optimizations below target the gemm region. The init_* loops can
    # optionally be parallelized or vectorized similarly but are not
    # performance-critical compared to GEMM.

    # ---------------- Data-layout optimization ------------------------------
    # B is stored column-major (as specified in data:), so that for fixed j
    # the access pattern B[k, j] in the k-reduction is unit-stride.
    # A is row-major, so A[i, k] is also unit-stride in k.
    # This enables efficient SIMD FMA along k with good spatial locality.

    # ---------------- 3D blocking / tiling ---------------------------------
    # Tile all three dimensions. I,J,K are tile indices; i,j,k remain the
    # intra-tile indices:
    #   i = I * TI + i_local,  j = J * TJ + j_local,  k = K * TK + k_local.
    # C tiles are TI x TJ; each is updated using A panels (TI x TK) and
    # B panels (TK x TJ).
    block(i, I, TI)
    block(j, J, TJ)
    block(k, K, TK)

    # Execute tiles in I–J–K order:
    #   for I, J: choose a C block
    #     for K: sweep along k with panels of A and B, accumulating into C
    # Within a fixed (I,J,K), the loops over i,j,k walk the tile data.
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)
    hoist(K)

    #   tmp = beta * C[i,j]           # scale once
    #   acc = sum_{k in tile K} A[i,k] * B[k,j]  # scalar accumulator in regs
    #   C[i,j] = tmp + alpha * acc
    # and accumulate across all K tiles. This preserves
    #   C[i,j] = beta * C_old[i,j] + alpha * sum_{k=0..NK-1} A[i,k]*B[k,j]
    # while loading/storing C[i,j] minimally and keeping the reduction in

    # Vectorize the innermost k-loop inside each tile. Because both
    # A[i,k] and B[k,j] are unit-stride in k (row-major A, column-major B),
    # the compiler can generate wide SIMD FMAs.
    vectorize(k, VEC_K)

    # Unroll the j-loop inside a tile so that several C[i, j+offset] values
    # are updated in registers simultaneously. This creates a small register
    # block for C and lets each k-vector be reused across multiple columns.
    unroll(j, UNROLL_J)

    # Parallelize across independent tiles of C. Different (I,J) tiles
    # update disjoint submatrices of C and read-only subregions of A and B,
    # so there are no write-write races or dependences between tiles.

    parallelize(J)

```text
# High-level model of GEMM kernel:
#   C := beta * C + alpha * A * B
# matching the semantics of kernel_gemm in the given Noarr code.

domain:
    i: dim in [0, NI)      # rows of A and C
    j: dim in [0, NJ)      # columns of B and C
    k: dim in [0, NK)      # columns of A / rows of B

data:
    # All three matrices are stored in row-major form, consistent with the
    # Noarr layouts:
    #   C: j_vec ^ i_vec  => dims (i, j), j contiguous
    #   A: k_vec ^ i_vec  => dims (i, k), k contiguous
    #   B: j_vec ^ k_vec  => dims (k, j), j contiguous

    A[i, k]: in num_t
        = (i, k) -> i * NK + k        # row-major: inner dim k is contiguous

    B[k, j]: in num_t
        = (k, j) -> k * NJ + j        # row-major: inner dim j is contiguous

    C[i, j]: inout num_t
        = (i, j) -> i * NJ + j        # row-major: inner dim j is contiguous

parameters:
    alpha: num_t
    beta:  num_t

computation:
    # Fused version of the two loops in kernel_gemm:
    #   1) C[i,j] *= beta;
    #   2) C[i,j] += alpha * sum_k (A[i,k] * B[k,j]);
    # This single assignment is pointwise equivalent to the original code:
    #   C[i,j] ← beta * C[i,j] + alpha * Σ_k A[i,k] * B[k,j].
    for i, j:
        C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j] +
                   alpha * sum(k in [0, NK), A[i, k] * B[k, j])


optimization:
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Tuning parameters (compile-time / configuration constants)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # TI, TJ, TK: tile sizes in i, j, k. Choose them so that:
    #   TI * TK * sizeof(num_t) and TK * TJ * sizeof(num_t) fit in L2/L3,
    #   and TI * TJ is large enough to amortize overhead.
    # VJ: SIMD width for the j-dimension (contiguous in C and B).
    # UK: unroll factor for the reduction over k.
    #
    # Example starting point for a 32-core x86_64 with AVX2 (doubles):
    #   TI = 128, TJ = 128, TK = 32, VJ = 4, UK = 4
    #
    # (Exact values are hardware- and problem-size-dependent.)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1) Cache blocking (tiling) in all three dimensions
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Split each logical dimension into an outer tile index (I,J,K) and
    # an inner index within the tile (still named i,j,k). This does not
    # change semantics; it only refines the iteration space.
    block(i, I, TI)      # i = I * TI + i_local
    block(j, J, TJ)      # j = J * TJ + j_local
    block(k, K, TK)      # k = K * TK + k_local

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2) Loop ordering / hoisting of tile loops
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Execute tiles in the order:
    #   outer:   I, J    (tiles of C)
    #   middle:  K       (tiles along the reduction dimension)
    #   inner:   i, k, j
    #
    # This maximizes temporal locality:
    #   - A tile C[I,I+TI)×[J,J+TJ) stays in cache while we sweep K.
    #   - Each A- and B-tile loaded for a given K is reused across many
    #     C elements in that (I,J) tile.
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)
    hoist(K)

    # Conceptual inner structure within one (I,J,K) tile after hoisting:
    #
    #   for i in tile(I):
    #     for k in tile(K):
    #       a_ik = A[i, k]                  # kept in a register
    #       for j in tile(J):               # contiguous in C and B
    #         C[i, j] += alpha * a_ik * B[k, j]
    #
    # and, before accumulating over all K tiles:
    #
    #   for i in tile(I):
    #     for j in tile(J):
    #       C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j]       # fused into the same nest logically

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3) Parallelization across independent tiles
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Different (I,J) tiles update disjoint submatrices of C, so they can
    # be computed in parallel without synchronization. Parallelizing over
    # I and J exposes coarse-grain parallelism for a 2D thread grid.
    #
    # A typical implementation would map:
    #   - I to "outer" parallelism (e.g., OpenMP outer loop),
    #   - J to inner parallelism or static scheduling within each I.
    parallelize(I)
    parallelize(J)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4) Vectorization and unrolling within tiles
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # j is the contiguous dimension in both C and B (row-major layout);
    # vectorizing along j gives unit-stride accesses for these arrays.
    # k is the reduction dimension; unrolling over k increases ILP and
    # lets the compiler schedule multiple FMA chains.
    vectorize(j, VJ)     # SIMD over columns of the current C-tile
    unroll(k, UK)        # unroll the inner reduction over k_local

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5) Scalar hoisting and reuse (micro-kernel behavior)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Within the innermost loops, for a fixed (i,k) pair in a tile:
    #   - hoist A[i,k] into a scalar 'a_ik' in a register,
    #   - reuse it across all j in the tile(J) loop,
    #   - reuse alpha as a scalar constant in registers.
    #
    # This reduces memory traffic for A and avoids redundant multiplies
    # by alpha, while leaving the mathematical expression unchanged:
    #
    #   for i in tile(I):
    #     for k in tile(K):
    #       a_ik = A[i,k]
    #       scaled_a_ik = alpha * a_ik
    #       for j in tile(J):      # vectorized
    #         C[i,j] = beta * C[i,j] (once per (i,j)) +
    #                  scaled_a_ik * B[k,j]
    #
    # (The "beta * C[i,j]" part is executed once per (i,j), logically
    # fused with the first K-tile; this matches the original semantics.)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 6) Optional packing into temporary tiles (within 50% memory overhead)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # For better cache/TLB behavior and prefetching, an implementation may:
    #
    #   - Allocate temporary tiles:
    #       A_block[TI, TK], B_block[TK, TJ]
    #   - For each (I,J,K) tile:
    #       * copy A[I:I+TI, K:K+TK] into A_block
    #       * copy B[K:K+TK, J:J+TJ] into B_block
    #       * run the micro-kernel on A_block, B_block, and C-tile
    #
    # This does not modify the mathematical result (it only changes where
    # data are read from) and, for reasonable TI,TJ,TK, A_block and
    # B_block together are much smaller than the full matrices, keeping
    # extra memory usage comfortably below 50% of the original footprint.
```

```text
domain:
    # Problem dimensions from NI, NJ, NK
    i: dim in [0, NI)   # row index of A and C
    j: dim in [0, NJ)   # column index of B and C
    k: dim in [0, NK)   # shared inner dimension of A and B

data:
    # Layouts are chosen to match or improve on the Noarr layouts.
    # The original C++ uses row-major for all three matrices:
    #   A: scalar ^ vector<'k'> ^ vector<'i'>   => addr = i*NK + k
    #   B: scalar ^ vector<'j'> ^ vector<'k'>   => addr = k*NJ + j
    #   C: scalar ^ vector<'j'> ^ vector<'i'>   => addr = i*NJ + j
    #
    # We keep A and C row-major and also keep B row-major (this matches the
    # current code and is friendly to an i–k–j traversal where j is innermost).

    A[i, k]: in  DATA_TYPE = (i, k) -> i * NK + k        # row-major: rows over k
    B[k, j]: in  DATA_TYPE = (k, j) -> k * NJ + j        # row-major: rows over j
    C[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NJ + j      # row-major: rows over j

parameters:
    # Scalar coefficients (fixed by init_array)
    alpha: DATA_TYPE = 1.5
    beta:  DATA_TYPE = 1.2

    # Tunable optimization parameters (compile-time or runtime constants):
    TI: int   # tile size along i (e.g., 128)
    TJ: int   # tile size along j (e.g., 128)
    TK: int   # tile size along k (e.g., 32)
    VJ: int   # SIMD width along j (e.g., 8 or 16 depending on DATA_TYPE and ISA)
    UK: int   # unroll factor for k (e.g., 4 or 8)

computation:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Initialization (matches init_array exactly)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    init_C:
        for i, j:
            # C[i][j] = (i*j + 1) % ni / ni, where ni = NI
            C[i, j] = ((i * j + 1) mod NI) / NI

    init_A:
        for i, k:
            # A[i][k] = i*(k+1) % nk / nk, where nk = NK
            A[i, k] = (i * (k + 1) mod NK) / NK

    init_B:
        for k, j:
            # B[k][j] = k*(j+2) % nj / nj, where nj = NJ
            B[k, j] = (k * (j + 2) mod NJ) / NJ

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # GEMM kernel: C := alpha * A * B + beta * C
    # This is mathematically equivalent to the two-phase kernel:
    #   1) C[i,j] *= beta
    #   2) C[i,j] += alpha * sum_k(A[i,k]*B[k,j])
    # but expressed in a fused form so we can load/store C[i,j]
    # only once per element.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    gemm:
        for i, j:
            C[i, j] =
                beta * C[i, j]
                + alpha * sum(k in [0, NK), A[i, k] * B[k, j])

optimization:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # High-level goal:
    #   Implement gemm as a cache-friendly, vectorized, and
    #   parallel 3D tiled kernel while preserving the mathematical
    #   semantics of C := alpha*A*B + beta*C.
    #
    # The key ideas:
    #   * 3D blocking over (i, j, k) for cache locality.
    #   * Loop order I–J–K–i–k–j so that:
    #       - We work on TI×TJ tiles of C at a time.
    #       - For fixed (i, k) we reuse A[i,k] across the whole j-tile.
    #       - For fixed (k, j) we reuse B[k,j] across the whole i-tile.
    #   * Accumulate each C[i,j] in a register across all k, then
    #     write it back once (fusing the beta scaling with the sum).
    #   * Parallelize across i-tiles (and optionally j-tiles).
    #   * Vectorize across j (the innermost, contiguous dimension).
    #   * Unroll the k-loop for more ILP and better FMA utilization.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    # 1. 3D blocking (tiling) of the GEMM loops.
    #    This turns:
    #        for i, j:
    #          C[i,j] = beta*C[i,j] + alpha * sum_k(...)
    #    into:
    #        for I in blocks of i with size TI:
    #          for J in blocks of j with size TJ:
    #            for K in blocks of k with size TK:
    #              for i in I, j in J, k in K: ...
    #
    #    The new tile indices (I, J, K) index tiles; the original
    #    i, j, k become intra-tile indices.
    block(i, I, TI)
    block(j, J, TJ)
    block(k, K, TK)

    # 2. Loop ordering:
    #    Hoist the tile loops so that the execution order is:
    #      outer:   I, then J, then K
    #      inner:   (within each tile) i, k, j
    #
    #    Hoisting I,J,K makes each (I,J) tile of C the unit of work
    #    and lets us traverse K in chunks that fit in cache:
    #      for I:
    #        for J:
    #          for K:
    #            for i in I:
    #              for k in K:
    #                for j in J:
    #                  ...
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)
    hoist(K)

    # 3. Ensure that within a tile, the innermost loop runs over j.
    #    This matches the row-major layouts:
    #      - C[i,j] is contiguous along j.
    #      - B[k,j] is contiguous along j (row-major).
    #    We keep k as the next-inner loop so that we can:
    #      - Reuse A[i,k] (scalar) across the whole j-tile.
    #      - Stream along rows of B and C with unit stride.
    #
    #    Conceptually, within each (I,J,K) tile we want:
    #      for i in I:
    #        for k in K:
    #          a_ik = alpha * A[i,k]
    #          for j in J:
    #            C[i,j] = C[i,j] + a_ik * B[k,j]
    #
    #    The interchange directive expresses the reordering of the
    #    innermost two loops from (..., j, k) to (..., k, j).
    interchange(k, j)

    # 4. Accumulate C[i,j] in registers and fuse beta scaling.
    #    # For each (i,j) in a tile, implement gemm as:
    #    #   acc = beta * C[i,j]           # scale once
    #    #   for all K-tiles, for k in K:  # full k-range
    #    #       acc += alpha * A[i,k] * B[k,j]
    #    #   C[i,j] = acc                  # single store
    #    #
    #    # This reduces memory traffic on C: one load + one store
    #    # per element instead of repeatedly loading/storing inside
    #    # the k-loop. It is an implementation detail inside the
    #    # tiled loops, so we describe it as a comment rather than
    #    # a separate directive.

    # 5. Vectorization along j.
    #    Since j is innermost and C/B are row-major, the j-loop
    #    accesses C[i, j..j+VJ-1] and B[k, j..j+VJ-1] with unit stride.
    #    This maps directly to SIMD loads/stores.
    #
    #    The compiler can then generate code of the form:
    #      load vecC  = C[i, j..j+VJ-1]
    #      for k in K-block:
    #        broadcast a_ik
    #        load vecB = B[k, j..j+VJ-1]
    #        vecC += a_ik * vecB
    #      store vecC back
    vectorize(j, VJ)

    # 6. Unroll the k-loop.
    #    Unrolling k by a small factor UK:
    #      * Increases instruction-level parallelism (ILP),
    #      * Lets the compiler schedule multiple FMAs per iteration,
    #      * Reduces loop overhead.
    #
    #    Since k is not the innermost loop after interchange, the
    #    unrolled body will contain VJ-wide vector ops over j for
    #    several consecutive k values.
    unroll(k, UK)

    # 7. Parallelization.
    #    Tiles corresponding to different I (and optionally J) do not
    #    share any elements of C, so they are embarrassingly parallel.
    #    We map outer tiles to threads/cores:
    #
    #      parallel for I:
    #        for J:
    #          for K:
    #            ... inner loops ...
    #
    #    This matches well with a 32-core machine: we choose TI large
    #    enough that each I-tile does substantial work, and TJ/TK
    #    tuned so that the working set of a tile fits in L2/L3 cache.
    parallelize(I)
    # (Optionally, if NI is small and NJ large, we could also
    #  parallelize(J) or use hierarchical parallelism over (I,J).)

    # 8. No extra large buffers beyond the original A,B,C.
    #    # Small stack-allocated temporaries for micro-kernels
    #    # (e.g., a handful of scalars or very small fixed-size
    #    # register tiles) are allowed but no additional matrices,
    #    # so total memory stays within the 1.5× budget.
```

domain:
    # Problem sizes match NI, NJ, NK used in the C++ code
    i: dim in [0, NI)      # rows of A and C
    j: dim in [0, NJ)      # columns of B and C
    k: dim in [0, NK)      # shared dimension between A and B

data:
    # Layouts are logical (i,j,k) indices plus an affine address expression.
    # We keep A and C row‑major and make B column‑major to improve k‑loop locality.

    # A is NI x NK, accessed as A[i, k]
    # Row-major: A[i, k] for fixed i is contiguous in k.
    A[i, k]: in DATA_TYPE =
        (i, k) -> i * NK + k

    # B is NK x NJ, accessed as B[k, j]
    # Column-major: for fixed j, B[0..NK-1, j] is contiguous in k.
    # This matches an innermost loop over k, giving unit-stride loads for B.
    B[k, j]: in DATA_TYPE =
        (k, j) -> k + j * NK

    # C is NI x NJ, accessed as C[i, j]
    # Row-major: for fixed i, C[i, 0..NJ-1] is contiguous in j.
    C[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE =
        (i, j) -> i * NJ + j

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE
    beta:  DATA_TYPE

    # Tunable blocking (tiling) and vectorization parameters.
    # They can be set based on cache sizes and SIMD width of the target machine.
    TI: int   # tile size along i (rows of C / A)
    TJ: int   # tile size along j (cols of C / B)
    TK: int   # tile size along k (shared dimension)
    VK: int   # SIMD width for vectorization along k

computation:
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Array initialization (matches init_array; included for completeness).
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    init_C:
        for i, j:
            # C[i][j] = (i*j + 1) % NI / NI
            C[i, j] = ((i * j + 1) mod NI) / NI

    init_A:
        for i, k:
            # A[i][k] = i*(k+1) % NK / NK
            A[i, k] = (i * (k + 1) mod NK) / NK

    init_B:
        for k, j:
            # B[k][j] = k*(j+2) % NJ / NJ
            B[k, j] = (k * (j + 2) mod NJ) / NJ

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # GEMM kernel: C := alpha * A * B + beta * C
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------

    scale_C:
        # First scale C by beta, as in the original kernel's first for_each.
        # This is elementwise and fully parallel over (i, j).
        for i, j:
            C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j]

    gemm:
        # Then perform the matrix multiplication A*B, scaled by alpha,
        # and accumulate into the already scaled C.
        #
        # Original code:
        #   for each i:
        #     for each j: C[i,j] *= beta;    // already modeled in scale_C
        #     for each (k,j): C[i,j] += alpha * A[i,k] * B[k,j];
        #
        # Mathematically this is equivalent to:
        for i, j:
            C[i, j] = C[i, j] + alpha * sum(k, A[i, k] * B[k, j])

        # This preserves the functional behavior of the C++ kernel (modulo
        # floating-point reassociation), while exposing a clear i–j–k structure.

optimization:
    # =========================================================================
    # Memory layout rationale
    # =========================================================================
    # - A and C are row-major: good reuse when iterating j inside i, or k inside i.
    # - B is column-major: for fixed j, B[k, j] is contiguous in k. With an
    #   innermost k-loop, both A[i, k] and B[k, j] are unit-stride in memory.
    #   This reduces cache misses and enables wide SIMD loads/stores.

    # =========================================================================
    # Loop structure and blocking (tiling)
    # =========================================================================
    # Tile all three dimensions so that:
    #   - each (TI x TJ) tile of C fits in L1/L2 and is updated repeatedly,
    #   - corresponding tiles of A (TI x TK) and B (TK x TJ) fit in cache,
    #   - we sweep over the k-tiles (K) to accumulate into C[I, J].
    #
    # We conceptually transform the gemm part into:
    #   for I in 0..NI step TI:
    #     for J in 0..NJ step TJ:
    #       for K in 0..NK step TK:
    #         for i in I..I+TI:
    #           for j in J..J+TJ:
    #             for k in K..K+TK:
    #               C[i,j] += alpha * A[i,k] * B[k,j];
    #
    # where the last incomplete tiles are truncated to the domain bounds.

    block(i, I, TI)   # introduce block index I and inner index i  (rows)
    block(j, J, TJ)   # introduce block index J and inner index j  (cols)
    block(k, K, TK)   # introduce block index K and inner index k  (inner dim)

    # Choose a standard blocked loop order:
    #   I (outermost) -> J -> K -> i -> j -> k (innermost)
    # so each C[I,J] tile is updated by sweeping all K-tiles.
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)
    hoist(K)

    # =========================================================================
    # Arithmetic optimization inside the k-tile
    # =========================================================================
    # Within a fixed (i, K) pair, alpha * A[i, k] is invariant w.r.t. j and
    # can be computed once per (i,k) and reused for all j in the current J-tile.
    #
    # Pseudocode inside a given (I,J,K) tile:
    #   for i in tile(I):
    #     for k in tile(K):
    #       a_ik = alpha * A[i, k]      # precompute scaled A
    #       for j in tile(J):
    #         C[i, j] += a_ik * B[k, j]
    #
    # This reduces the number of multiplications by ~50% in the innermost nest
    # without introducing any new arrays (a_ik is a scalar register).
    #
    # In the model, this is an algebraic optimization of the per-iteration
    # expression for C[i,j].

    # =========================================================================
    # Vectorization
    # =========================================================================
    # With B column-major and A row-major, both A[i, k] and B[k, j] are
    # contiguous in the innermost k-loop. We explicitly vectorize k:
    vectorize(k, VK)
    # where VK is chosen to match the SIMD width (e.g., 8 for AVX2 float,
    # 16 for AVX-512 float). The compiler can then emit wide loads/stores
    # and FMA instructions for:
    #   a_ik_vec  = alpha * A[i, k..k+VK-1]
    #   b_vec     = B[k..k+VK-1, j]
    #   acc_vec  += a_ik_vec * b_vec

    # Optionally unroll the inner j loop within a tile to increase ILP and
    # better hide memory latency for B and C:
    unroll(j, 4)

    # =========================================================================
    # Parallelization
    # =========================================================================
    # Each element C[i, j] depends only on:
    #   - its previous value C[i, j] (after scaling by beta), and
    #   - A[i, *] and B[*, j].
    # Hence different (i, j) pairs are independent after scale_C completes.
    #
    # We parallelize over the outer i-blocks I (and optionally J) so that
    # each thread owns disjoint tiles of C and the corresponding tiles of
    # A and B. No synchronization is needed between threads during gemm.

    parallelize(I)    # e.g., map I-tiles to OpenMP threads

    # Optionally, for very large NJ, 2D tiling can be used:
    # parallelize(J)
    # (Each (I, J) tile is exclusive to a thread, so there are no write races
    # on C and no need for reductions.)

    # Note: we do NOT parallelize along k, because that would require a
    # reduction over partial C tiles. By parallelizing along I (and possibly J)
    # only, each C[i, j] is updated by exactly one thread.
